extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, courts, and policymakers dealing with prior art, novelty and inventive step
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining whether information (including paperless/internet disclosures, confidential disclosures, and physical devices) forms part of the prior art for assessing novelty and inventive step in patent law, with comparative notes from Australia, Belgium and Brazil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single non-confidential disclosure suffices for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A single, non-confidential disclosure is sufficient for the purposes of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More widespread distribution or at least ability to be located is required to meet the test for inventive step. For novelty the prior art is considered as read by the ordinarily skilled person in the art — the question is whether he would understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge (CGK) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To amount to common general knowledge, the information must be well known to the relevant skilled workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The person skilled in the art is treated as reading the prior art; inventive step analysis uses the specific requirements for CGK (see referenced Section A(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential disclosure not prior art (unless offer for sale)
rubrics_metrics.description: A confidential disclosure is not considered to form part of the prior art unless it amounts to an offer for sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality status of a disclosure determines whether it is treated as prior art; practical tests consider whether the information was subject to obligations of confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering/disassembly can constitute disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a device could in principle be disassembled or reverse engineered, and the device is made publicly available, then this is likely to be a disclosure of any invention embodied in the device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For novelty, unless all elements are disclosed as the document would be read by the person skilled in the art, there is not sufficient disclosure. Actual public use of a device to perform its function may disclose inventions not directly presented to public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperless/electronic (internet) information can be prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperless information (e.g. on an electronic network or the internet) does constitute a disclosure which, subject to meeting statutory requirements such as date of public availability, is sufficient to affect novelty and/or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions at the patent office and courts have treated paperless disclosures as suitable prior art; difficulties arise not from paperless form itself but from proving statutory requirements (dates, form).

rubrics_metrics.name: No substantive statutory difference for paperless disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no differences in the statutory requirements given to paperless information compared to other traditional forms of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peculiarities of electronic media principally alter how paperless information is shown to meet statutory requirements (e.g., proof of content/date), rather than altering the substantive requirements themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption alone does not preserve confidentiality for novelty/inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Encrypted information is not likely to be considered as providing a higher level of confidentiality compared to non-encrypted information; whether it is confidential depends on obligations of confidence, not encryption per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encryption makes accidental disclosure less likely, but unless recipients are bound by confidentiality obligations the encrypted information may nevertheless constitute a disclosure. Email will be considered confidential if, in the circumstances, it is reasonable to expect the information was provided in confidence (practice: confidentiality clause in emails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access controls (passwords, paywalls, search limitations) affect disclosure only via accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Passwords, search engines and payment requirements influence whether paperless information is confidential or available as a disclosure for novelty and inventive step by affecting public accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms are relevant only insofar as they operate to fetter who can access the information; without obligations of confidentiality they do not on their own confine the information as confidential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure for internet material (downloading location principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The place of disclosure in relation to information placed on the internet may be the place at which the information is downloaded (Gutnick v. Dow Jones), but for novelty publication anywhere in the world makes a document relevant prior art subject to date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gutnick is a defamation case and its applicability to patents is limited; however, paperless information that satisfies other criteria will be prior art for novelty once it is available publicly on the internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step/place considerations (local CGK vs worldwide documents)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventive step attacks one can rely on: (i) the common general knowledge (CGK) as it existed in the patent area before the priority date, or (ii) the CGK together with documents published anywhere in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a document to establish CGK it almost certainly needs wide publication in the patent area (e.g., Australia). If combining documents with CGK under (ii), the place of disclosure of those documents is less important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and duration requirements for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no special timing/duration statutory requirements for electronic availability beyond that the disclosure must predate the priority date and be accessible to the public; availability for only seconds is unlikely to satisfy the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration impacts whether the information constitutes a disclosure on a case-by-case basis; the critical point is that timing predates the priority date and duration enables public access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archives and contemporaneous records necessary to prove internet content
rubrics_metrics.description: Archives are necessary to establish the form the information took at a particular date; absence of archives is a major problem in using internet material as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paperless information is easily manipulated; without an archive establishing the content at the relevant date internet material has been dismissed in several Patent Office cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for establishing prior art (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting that a piece of information was disclosed (i.e., the opponent) bears the burden of proof, and the standard is the civil standard — balance of probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the Patent Office the practice gives benefit of the doubt to the applicant; the Patents Bill may require applicants to positively demonstrate novelty and inventive step, but in opposition it remains incumbent on the opponent to establish prior art on the balance of probabilities. In court revocation proceedings the burden lies with the party asserting invalidity and the standard remains balance of probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary procedures: Patent Office vs courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings before the Patent Office are not subject to the same evidentiary formalities as courts (e.g., hearsay is admissible before the Patent Office); courts generally require stricter proof though have limited powers to dispense with formal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Court can relax rules where matters are not bona fide in dispute or where strict compliance would cause unnecessary expense/delay, but it is unlikely to dispense with proving existence/date of publication of prior art that goes to patent validity. Trend is to admit all relevant evidence subject to reliability and weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special evidence rules for internet disclosures; apply existing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no special rules of evidence specifically for establishing internet disclosures; the usual rules of evidence apply and the party relying on the disclosure must prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given potential manipulation and transient nature of internet material courts may take into account gravity and nature of the matter (e.g., s140(2) Evidence Act 1995) when deciding whether the balance of probabilities is met. Existing rules are viewed as providing a reasonable balance between certainty and flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian Group proposed essential elements for harmonisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Three elements considered essential for a common definition/standard of prior art disclosure: (i) a definition of the prior art; (ii) principles by which novelty is established (may include requirement that prior art provide clear and unmistakable directions to perform the invention); (iii) principles by which obviousness/inventive step is established (may include focusing on underlying/basic knowledge of the skilled person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Australian Group is reluctant to propose harmonisation until other national group views are known; these three are suggested as essential building blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belgian law: accessibility is the criterion for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Belgian law the criterion applied for whether something is prior art is accessibility (art.5 §2); there is no exclusion of means of disclosure and the place of disclosure is irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date of disclosure is irrelevant for novelty but can influence inventive step. Confidentiality obligations are governed by general law. Access restrictions (passwords, keys) are relevant only insofar as they affect accessibility. Archives/duration of electronic availability are of no consequence, but the date must be determinable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belgian rule on pending applications and differences between novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Belgian law treats the content of certain pending applications (e.g., Belgian patent, European patent designating Belgium, PCT designating Belgium) as part of the state of the art for novelty but not for inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law makes a limited list of pending applications that are included for novelty; inventive step uses a different criterion and does not include pending applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brazil: novelty requires single-document disclosure; inventive step may combine documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Brazilian law, to prove lack of novelty it is necessary that all elements of the claimed invention be disclosed in a single document; for inventive step it is possible to submit several pieces of prior art to prove lack of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 11 defines state of the art as everything made accessible to the public prior to filing date by any means, in Brazil or abroad. Administrative practice indicates documents with restricted circulation (e.g., internal factory documents or exchanges between two companies) are not considered accessible to the public.
